y-m-06-01.title: Can we trust the result of sorting the buttons?
y-m-06-01.topic: Sorting: choosing a rule and checking the result
y-m-06-01.goal: Pick out the sorting rules that give the same result no matter who sorts, find the place in a sorted result that does not fit the rule and fix it, and then sort by a different rule yourself.
y-m-06-01.material:
Harin wants to sort 8 buttons into two groups. The color, shape, and number of holes of each button are in the table below.
Button 1: red / circle / 2 holes
Button 2: blue / circle / 4 holes
Button 3: red / square / 4 holes
Button 4: yellow / circle / 2 holes
Button 5: blue / square / 2 holes
Button 6: yellow / square / 4 holes
Button 7: red / circle / 4 holes
Button 8: blue / circle / 2 holes
Harin sorted by the number of holes and wrote down the result. Check whether the result can be trusted, and also sort by a different rule.
y-m-06-01.thinking.0: Checking whether the sorting rule is clear
y-m-06-01.thinking.1: Finding errors in a sorted result and a wrong way of checking
y-m-06-01.thinking.2: Sorting by a different rule yourself
y-m-06-01.prereq.0: Having sorted things by color, shape, and number
y-m-06-01.prereq.1: How to read each cell of a table
y-m-06-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the rules that give the same result no matter who sorts. (You can only use what is written in the table.)
y-m-06-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each rule, imagine whether two friends who sort separately would get the same result.
y-m-06-01.s.s1.hint.1: Look one by one for whether what each rule uses is written in the table.
y-m-06-01.s.s1.o.a: Whether it has 2 holes or 4 holes
y-m-06-01.s.s1.r.a: If you read the number of holes in the table, anyone puts a button in the same group. You noticed that the rule is clear.
y-m-06-01.s.s1.o.b: Whether it is a prettier button or not
y-m-06-01.s.s1.r.b: What feels pretty is different for each person, so the same button could go in different groups.
y-m-06-01.s.s1.o.c: Whether it is a big button or a small button
y-m-06-01.s.s1.r.c: The table has no size, and it is not decided how big counts as big. Different people could sort differently.
y-m-06-01.s.s1.o.d: Whether it is Harin's favorite color or not
y-m-06-01.s.s1.r.d: Someone who does not know Harin's feelings cannot sort. It is not decided from the table alone.
y-m-06-01.s.s1.o.e: Whether the shape is a circle or a square
y-m-06-01.s.s1.r.e: If you read the shape column of the table, anyone gets the same result. You noticed that there is one more clear rule.
y-m-06-01.s.s1.explain: The number of holes and the shape written in the table can be read, so anyone can put a button in the same group. Whether it is pretty, big, or liked changes with the person or situation or is not in the table, so we cannot say the same result comes out.
y-m-06-01.s.s2.hint.0: Find each button written in the groups in the table one by one and check its number of holes.
y-m-06-01.s.s2.line.0: Rule: Sort into buttons with 2 holes and buttons with 4 holes.
y-m-06-01.s.s2.line.3: 5 and 3 together make 8, and there are 8 buttons in all, so the result is correct.
y-m-06-01.s.s2.explain: Line 2 includes Button 7, but in the table Button 7 has 4 holes. So this line is wrong. Line 4 said "the count is 8, so the result is correct too," but even if the count is right, a button can still be in the wrong group. The correct result is 2 holes: Buttons 1, 4, 5, 8; 4 holes: Buttons 2, 3, 6, 7. Line 1 and line 3 are correct.
y-m-06-01.s.s3.prompt: Sort the 8 buttons into two groups by a rule other than the number of holes. Write the rule and the button numbers in each group, and also write why anyone sorting would get the same result.
y-m-06-01.s.s3.hint.0: Pick either the color column or the shape column of the table and gather the numbers of the ones that are the same.
y-m-06-01.s.s3.hint.1: After writing all the numbers in the two groups, count whether all 8 are included.
y-m-06-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The rule is ... The ... group is Buttons ..., ...
y-m-06-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Could another person sort the buttons by reading only my rule?
y-m-06-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check each button number you wrote against the table?
y-m-06-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is there any button that is missing or that is in both groups?
y-m-06-01.s.s3.model.0: I sorted by color. The red group is Buttons 1, 3, 7 and the not-red group is Buttons 2, 4, 5, 6, 8. You can tell color right away by looking, so it is the same no matter who sorts.
y-m-06-01.s.s3.model.1: I sorted by shape. Circles are Buttons 1, 2, 4, 7, 8 and squares are Buttons 3, 5, 6. Whether it is a circle or a square looks the same to everyone.
y-m-06-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: Sorting into three groups, blue, yellow, and red, is also a fine different way of sorting.

y-m-06-02.title: Does our thinking change each time survey results arrive?
y-m-06-02.topic: Collecting data: statements that change with the number of people surveyed
y-m-06-02.goal: Compare the result from asking some people with the result from more people, realize that how much you can trust it changes, and find the cases where someone who has not yet answered could change the result.
y-m-06-02.material: Class 3 of Grade 2 has 24 students in all. They want to choose a picnic snack from jelly, cookies, and bread, with each person choosing only one. The survey results arrive a little at a time. As you read the results that arrive, change your thinking about what would be good to choose, or leave it as it is.
y-m-06-02.thinking.0: Fixing your judgment or leaving it as it is, depending on the new data
y-m-06-02.thinking.1: Being careful about stretching a result from some people to the whole group
y-m-06-02.thinking.2: Finding the conditions under which the result changes
y-m-06-02.prereq.0: Comparing the sizes of numbers up to 20
y-m-06-02.prereq.1: Reading the number of students from a table
y-m-06-02.s.s1.prompt: Read the data in the order it arrives, and each time choose the judgment you can make now.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.hint.0: Compare whether the result that arrived this time supports or goes against the earlier judgment.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.hint.1: Count whether there are people who have not answered yet.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.0.info: First, 6 students were asked. 4 chose jelly, 1 chose cookies, and 1 chose bread. 18 students have not answered yet.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: With this result, what should we do about the snack for the class of 24?
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.0.after: Jelly looks ahead, but 18 students are still left, so it is too early to settle it as the whole class's result. Making a guess, and also asking more people, are both fine.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The most people chose jelly, so the whole class will also have the most for jelly.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This stretched the result of 6 students straight to the whole class. We do not know yet how the other 18 will choose.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Only 6 students were asked, so it is too early to choose the snack for the whole class.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This noticed that there are still many people we do not know about.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Jelly seems to be ahead, so make a guess for now and ask more people.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This thinking uses the current result as a basis for a guess, without settling it, and tries to find out more.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Cookies and bread have only 1 each, so leave them out as choices from the start.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This crossed out the small numbers as choices, even though we do not yet know what the rest of the people will choose.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.1.info: Now all 20 students who are present have been asked (including the first 6). 7 chose jelly, 9 chose cookies, and 4 chose bread.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: Choose what you can say from this result.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.1.after: The result from the first 6 students became weaker compared to the 20. Among the 20, you can say cookies are the most and bread is the fewest. To say something about all 24, it is still not enough.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Among the 20 students asked, the most people chose cookies.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This statement reads the result of the 20 just as it is.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: There was more jelly among the first 6, so jelly is the most.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This still trusts the result of the first 6. Compare it with the result of the 20 that just arrived.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The fewest of the 20 chose bread.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This statement compares the three numbers and reads them.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: 9 chose cookies, so decide that the class of 24 also has the most for cookies.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This stretched the result of 20 straight to the result of all 24. There are still people who have not come.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.2.info: But these 20 are the friends who are present. The 4 who were absent that day have not chosen yet. The result for 20 of the 24 is as above.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: What should we do to choose the snack?
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.2.after: The 4 absent students could change the result. In the next step, find out for yourself how much they could change it. The thought "go with cookies but say it may change" is fine, and the thought "ask the 4 first" is fine too.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The result may change depending on how the 4 absent students choose, so ask the 4 too.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This thinking considers whether the remaining people could change the result.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Cookies are the most now, so go with cookies, but say it may change depending on the result of the 4 absent students.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This uses the current result and also states the condition that it is not settled.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Decide on cookies, assuming the 4 absent students all chose cookies too.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: We do not know how the absent friends will choose, but this assumed they would be the same as the current result.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The result of the 20 cannot be trusted, so survey again from the beginning.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This threw away all the results already collected. Check whether it is enough to find out about only the 4 we do not know.
y-m-06-02.s.s1.reflect: The result of the first 6, the result of the 20 present, and the fact of the 4 who have not answered each changed "how much we can say." You do not have to stick to a judgment once you make it, and it is also a good way to say it with a condition that fits the current result.
y-m-06-02.s.s2.prompt: Say that each of the 4 absent students chooses only jelly or cookies (nobody chooses bread). If k of them choose jelly, then (4-k) of them choose cookies. When you add these 4 students' choices to the result of the 20 (jelly 7, cookies 9, bread 4), find two different values of k that make jelly equal to or more than cookies, and enter them.
y-m-06-02.s.s2.hint.0: Decide one value of k, and write on two lines how many students jelly and cookies each become.
y-m-06-02.s.s2.hint.1: Change k one by one from 0 to 4 and compare the two numbers.
y-m-06-02.s.s2.var.k: The number of the 4 absent students who chose jelly
y-m-06-02.s.s2.ok.c1: A whole-number count of people from 0 to 4.
y-m-06-02.s.s2.fail.c1: There are 4 absent students, so k must be one of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
y-m-06-02.s.s2.ok.c2: Jelly became equal to or more than cookies.
y-m-06-02.s.s2.fail.c2: In this case, jelly is less than cookies. Add k to the 7 for jelly and (4-k) to the 9 for cookies, and compare.
y-m-06-02.s.s2.explain: If k is 3, jelly is 10 and cookies are 10, so they are equal, and if k is 4, jelly is 11 and cookies are 9. If k is 2 or less, cookies stay ahead. So if 3 or more of the 4 absent students choose jelly, the result changes.

y-m-06-03.title: Are three pictures really 3 people?
y-m-06-03.topic: Picture graph: why you need to know the number one picture stands for
y-m-06-03.goal: Realize that to say a number of people from a picture graph, you need to know the number that one picture stands for. After getting that information, decide values in the picture graph that fit the conditions.
y-m-06-03.material:
The number of students who came to the library was shown by day in a picture graph. But the line under the graph that said "one ◯ is how many students" was erased. A half picture ◐ stands for half of ◯. Wednesday and Thursday have not been drawn yet.
Monday: ◯ ◯ ◯
Tuesday: ◯ ◯ ◐
Jeongwu counted the pictures and said, "Monday is 3 students."
y-m-06-03.thinking.0: Finding more information needed to say a number
y-m-06-03.thinking.1: Making several values that fit the conditions after information is available
y-m-06-03.thinking.2: Saying how to check a friend's statement
y-m-06-03.prereq.0: Counting the number of pictures in a picture graph
y-m-06-03.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of numbers up to 20
y-m-06-03.s.s1.prompt: To say how many students came on Monday, what is the first thing you need to know?
y-m-06-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write separately what you can see and what you cannot see in the Monday row.
y-m-06-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what agreement there must be for 3 pictures to mean 3 students.
y-m-06-03.s.s1.o.a: How many students one picture stands for
y-m-06-03.s.s1.r.a: You found the agreement that connects the number of pictures to the number of students.
y-m-06-03.s.s1.o.b: What grade the students who came on Monday are in
y-m-06-03.s.s1.r.b: Even if you know the grade, you cannot tell how many students one picture stands for.
y-m-06-03.s.s1.o.c: How many students who came on Monday borrowed a book
y-m-06-03.s.s1.r.c: Students who borrowed books and students who came are different. What we want to know now is the number of students who came.
y-m-06-03.s.s1.o.d: Whether the pictures are placed sideways or up and down
y-m-06-03.s.s1.r.d: The direction they are placed does not change the number.
y-m-06-03.s.s1.explain: We know the number of pictures, but whether one picture is 1 student, 2 students, or 5 students can only be known from the graph's explanation. That agreement was erased, so we cannot yet decide the number of students.
y-m-06-03.s.s2.prompt: It turned out that one ◯ is 2 students and one ◐ is 1 student (Monday 6 students, Tuesday 5 students). The students who came from Monday to Thursday are 20 in all. Make two different ways for the numbers of students who came on Wednesday and Thursday, which have not been drawn yet. Wednesday is more than Thursday, and Thursday is also at least 1 student.
y-m-06-03.s.s2.hint.0: First write the numbers of students for Monday and Tuesday, and think about how many students are left.
y-m-06-03.s.s2.hint.1: Decide one number for Wednesday and match Thursday to it, then check that Wednesday is more.
y-m-06-03.s.s2.var.w: Number of students who came on Wednesday
y-m-06-03.s.s2.var.t: Number of students who came on Thursday
y-m-06-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of students are natural numbers, and Thursday is also at least 1 student.
y-m-06-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of students must be natural numbers, and Thursday must be at least 1 student.
y-m-06-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The four days add up to 20 students.
y-m-06-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Monday's 6 students and Tuesday's 5 students together with Wednesday and Thursday must make 20 students.
y-m-06-03.s.s2.fail.c3: Wednesday must be more than Thursday.
y-m-06-03.s.s2.explain: Wednesday + Thursday is 9 students and Wednesday is more, so (8,1), (7,2), (6,3), and (5,4) are possible. An odd number can be drawn using one ◐. For example, 7 students is 3 ◯ and 1 ◐.
y-m-06-03.s.s3.prompt: Tell Jeongwu how he could check the statement "There are 3 pictures, so it is 3 students." Also write why you say so.
y-m-06-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write the number of students when there are 3 pictures, for the case where one picture is 1 student and for the case where it is 2 students.
y-m-06-03.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether the numbers of students in the two cases are the same.
y-m-06-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does "how many students one picture stands for" appear in your writing?
y-m-06-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write knowing that Jeongwu's statement may be right and may not be?
y-m-06-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is there a way of checking that Jeongwu can follow?
y-m-06-03.s.s3.model.0: You cannot say right away that 3 pictures means 3 students. First you need to know how many students one picture stands for. Look for the explanation under the graph.
y-m-06-03.s.s3.model.1: We cannot tell yet whether Jeongwu is right. One ◯ could be 2 students or 5 students, so let's check how many one picture is.

y-m-06-04.title: Finding the odd place in a vote result table
y-m-06-04.topic: Collecting data: comparing a tally count with the total number of people
y-m-06-04.goal: Find the wrong place in a count made with bundles and single marks, and explain that comparing the total number of marks in the result with the number of people who voted is a way of checking.
y-m-06-04.material:
Class 4 of Grade 2 has 29 students in all. During break time, each person raised a hand just once to choose a game to play. The teacher made one mark at a time on the board, and when 5 marks gathered, tied them into one bundle.
Tag: 1 bundle and 2 single marks
Jump rope: 1 bundle and 4 single marks
Dodgeball: 2 bundles and 3 single marks
Ara read the marks and wrote down the result. Look at Ara's writing.
y-m-06-04.thinking.0: Checking the reason for each line of the solution
y-m-06-04.thinking.1: Checking whether the result fits the overall condition
y-m-06-04.thinking.2: Explaining why the checking method is useful
y-m-06-04.prereq.0: How to read marks tied in groups of 5
y-m-06-04.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of numbers up to 30
y-m-06-04.s.s1.hint.0: In each line, check again how many votes one bundle is.
y-m-06-04.s.s1.line.0: Tag: 1 bundle and 2 single marks, so 5+2=7 votes
y-m-06-04.s.s1.line.1: Jump rope: 1 bundle and 4 single marks, so 5+4=9 votes
y-m-06-04.s.s1.line.2: Dodgeball: 2 bundles and 3 single marks, so 5+3=8 votes
y-m-06-04.s.s1.line.3: 7+9+8=24, so there are 24 votes in all.
y-m-06-04.s.s1.line.4: The class has 29 students but only 24 votes, so 5 students did not vote.
y-m-06-04.s.s2.prompt: Ara's total of 24 does not match the class's 29 students. What would be best to do first?
y-m-06-04.s.s2.hint.0: Point with your finger at each line on the board and read the number of bundles and single marks again.
y-m-06-04.s.s2.hint.1: Add up all the numbers of marks you read again and compare with whether they equal 29.
y-m-06-04.s.s2.o.a: Find the 5 students who did not vote and make them vote again.
y-m-06-04.s.s2.r.a: This blamed people before considering other reasons. It has not yet checked whether the counted result is right.
y-m-06-04.s.s2.o.b: Add 5 votes to Tag to make 29 votes.
y-m-06-04.s.s2.r.b: This made up votes to match the number. It matches with numbers, not with real votes.
y-m-06-04.s.s2.o.c: Count the bundles and single marks again on the board, line by line.
y-m-06-04.s.s2.r.c: This thinking tries to check the counted result again.
y-m-06-04.s.s2.o.d: It does not matter if the total is different, so leave it as it is.
y-m-06-04.s.s2.r.d: This noticed the difference and passed over it. It clashes with the condition that each person voted only once.
y-m-06-04.s.s2.explain: Each person voted only once, so the total number of all the votes must be 29. If it does not match, it is good to first check the counted result again.
y-m-06-04.s.s3.prompt: When each person voted only once, why is it useful to compare the total of all the votes with the number of students in the class? Write one or two sentences.
y-m-06-04.s.s3.hint.0: Imagine what would happen to the total number of votes if one person could raise a hand twice.
y-m-06-04.s.s3.hint.1: Write in words at least one reason why 29 and 24 are different.
y-m-06-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Each person votes once, so ...
y-m-06-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the condition "each person votes once" appear in your writing?
y-m-06-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say what happens if the total of the votes is different from the number of students in the class?
y-m-06-04.s.s3.model.0: Each person voted only once, so adding all the votes should equal the 29 students in the class. If it is different, something was counted wrong somewhere.
y-m-06-04.s.s3.model.1: If the number of votes and the number of people do not match, it means there is a mistake. If you check whether the total votes equal 29 students, you can tell whether there is a wrong line.

y-m-06-05.title: What is the smallest number of students the winner could have?
y-m-06-05.topic: Reading data: the relationship between the most chosen item and the total number of people
y-m-06-05.goal: Test the statement "the winner is at least half of the total" by making counterexamples, and work out how many students the winner must have at least for there to be only one winner.
y-m-06-05.material:
20 students each chose one school lunch menu from tteokbokki, gimbap, ramyeon, and dumplings. Each person chose only one. When there is only one menu that was chosen the most, we call that menu the "winner." If the same number is the most, we say there is no winner.
Jaei said, "The winning menu must be chosen by at least 10 students. It's half of 20."
y-m-06-05.thinking.0: Testing a general statement with a counterexample
y-m-06-05.thinking.1: Making several tables that follow the conditions
y-m-06-05.thinking.2: Finding the smallest case and stating the limit
y-m-06-05.prereq.0: Splitting numbers up to 20 into several parts
y-m-06-05.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of several numbers
y-m-06-05.s.s1.prompt: What would be a good way to find out whether Jaei's statement is always right?
y-m-06-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write in words what a table that is the exact opposite of Jaei's statement would look like.
y-m-06-05.s.s1.hint.1: Decide on one number of winner votes that would be good to test first.
y-m-06-05.s.s1.o.a: Make one more table where the winner has 10 students.
y-m-06-05.s.s1.r.a: The case of 10 already fits the statement. To find out whether there is a table that goes against the statement, you need to look for another case.
y-m-06-05.s.s1.o.b: Make a table where all four menus have the same number.
y-m-06-05.s.s1.r.b: If all are the same, there is no winner, so you cannot test the statement.
y-m-06-05.s.s1.o.c: Assume Jaei is right and look for the reason.
y-m-06-05.s.s1.r.c: If you start from the idea that it is right and only look for reasons, you may miss cases where the statement breaks.
y-m-06-05.s.s1.o.d: Make a table where the winner has fewer than 10 students.
y-m-06-05.s.s1.r.d: This thinking tries to make an example that goes against the statement yourself.
y-m-06-05.s.s1.explain: The word "must" is broken if you can make even one table that goes against it. Try to find a table where there is only one winner and it has fewer than 10 students.
y-m-06-05.s.s2.prompt: Make two different tables that show Jaei's statement is wrong. Tteokbokki must be the winner (it must have more than every other menu), tteokbokki has 9 students or fewer, and the four menus add up to 20 students.
y-m-06-05.s.s2.hint.0: Decide the number for tteokbokki and split the remaining students among the three menus.
y-m-06-05.s.s2.hint.1: Compare one by one whether all three menus are fewer than tteokbokki.
y-m-06-05.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of students are natural numbers that are 0 or more.
y-m-06-05.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of students must be natural numbers that are 0 or more.
y-m-06-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The four menus must add up to 20 students.
y-m-06-05.s.s2.ok.c3: Tteokbokki has more than all the other menus, so it is the winner.
y-m-06-05.s.s2.fail.c3: Tteokbokki must be more than each of gimbap, ramyeon, and dumplings.
y-m-06-05.s.s2.ok.c4: The winner has 9 students or fewer, so it goes against Jaei's statement.
y-m-06-05.s.s2.fail.c4: If the winner has 10 students or more, it is a case that fits Jaei's statement. Try 9 students or fewer.
y-m-06-05.s.s2.explain: For example, tteokbokki 6, gimbap 5, ramyeon 5, dumplings 4 add up to 20 students and tteokbokki is the winner, but it has fewer than 10. So the statement "the winner must have at least 10" is wrong. Tables where gimbap, ramyeon, and dumplings swap places count as the same case.
y-m-06-05.s.s3.prompt: When 20 students each choose one of four menus and there is only one winner, what is the smallest number of students who could have chosen the winning menu?
y-m-06-05.s.s3.hint.0: Set the winner at 5 students, and write the most the other three menus can have in total if they are all less than 5.
y-m-06-05.s.s3.r.a: If you split 20 students equally among four menus, it is 5 each. But if all are the same, there is not just one winner.
y-m-06-05.s.s3.r.b: If the winner has 5, the rest are all 4 or fewer, so it falls short. It becomes possible from 6 students.
y-m-06-05.s.s3.r.c: It is true that a table with 7 exists, but check whether a smaller number is also possible.
y-m-06-05.s.s3.r.d: 10 students is the value Jaei said. We just made a table with fewer.
y-m-06-05.s.s3.explain: If the winner has 5, the other three menus each have 4 or fewer, so 5+4+4+4=17 does not reach 20. With 6, you can make 6+5+5+4=20. So the winner has at least 6.

y-m-06-06.title: If two classes have different winners, is the combined winner one of those two?
y-m-06-06.topic: Combining data: the winners of two groups and the winner of the combined result
y-m-06-06.goal: Realize that many examples that fit do not guarantee "always," and make a case where, when the tables of two classes are combined, a fruit that was not the winner in either class becomes the winner.
y-m-06-06.material:
Class 1 and Class 2 each have 12 students. Every student chose only one of apple, tangerine, and pear. Say that in each class, there is only one fruit chosen the most.
Jihu said, "If the fruit chosen the most in Class 1 and the fruit chosen the most in Class 2 are different, then the fruit that is the most when the two classes are combined is one of those two."
Jihu checked three cases, and the statement was right all three times. One case is like this. Class 1: apple 5, tangerine 4, pear 3. Class 2: apple 3, tangerine 5, pear 4. (Combined it is apple 8, tangerine 9, pear 7, so the most is tangerine.)
y-m-06-06.thinking.0: Checking whether a general statement is right even with a few examples that fit
y-m-06-06.thinking.1: Making a table that is a counterexample yourself
y-m-06-06.prereq.0: Comparing the sizes of numbers up to 12
y-m-06-06.prereq.1: Adding the numbers of the same fruit from the tables and reading the total
y-m-06-06.s.s1.prompt: Jihu checked three cases and the statement was right in all of them. Can we say from this alone that Jihu's statement is always right?
y-m-06-06.s.s1.hint.0: Organize in a table which class's winner the combined winning fruit was in the three cases.
y-m-06-06.s.s1.hint.1: Write what a fruit that is not the winner in either class would have to look like in each class in order to become the most when combined.
y-m-06-06.s.s1.o.a: It was right three times, so we can say it is always right.
y-m-06-06.s.s1.r.a: This talked about every case just because a few examples fit. There are still cases that were not tested.
y-m-06-06.s.s1.o.b: Being right three times is no evidence at all.
y-m-06-06.s.s1.r.b: This saw a pile of examples that fit as meaning nothing. They do make you more confident, but they do not settle it.
y-m-06-06.s.s1.o.c: If we check ten more examples and all are right, we can say it is always right.
y-m-06-06.s.s1.r.c: Even if you collect more examples, untested cases remain. The number of times it was right cannot guarantee "always."
y-m-06-06.s.s1.o.d: We cannot know whether it is always right, so look for an example where it is wrong.
y-m-06-06.s.s1.r.d: This thinking separates the examples checked from the cases not checked.
y-m-06-06.s.s1.o.e: Jihu checked it himself, so trust it as it is.
y-m-06-06.s.s1.r.e: This thinking says the statement is right just because it was checked. It does not look at which cases were checked.
y-m-06-06.s.s1.explain: Even if there are many examples that fit, it can go against the statement in a case that was not tested. If you find one example that goes against it, "always" is broken. So it is good to look for an example where it is wrong and test it.
y-m-06-06.s.s2.prompt: Make a table that shows Jihu's statement is wrong. The winner of Class 1 must be apple, and the winner of Class 2 must be tangerine. When the two classes are combined, pear must be more than both apple and tangerine. Each class has 12 students. Enter two different tables. (Class 1: apple a1, tangerine b1, pear c1 / Class 2: apple a2, tangerine b2, pear c2)
y-m-06-06.s.s2.hint.0: First decide how many pear students each class should have so that pear is large when combined.
y-m-06-06.s.s2.hint.1: Split the remaining students between apple and tangerine, and check the winner condition for each class one at a time.
y-m-06-06.s.s2.ok.c1: All are natural numbers that are 0 or more.
y-m-06-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of students must be natural numbers that are 0 or more.
y-m-06-06.s.s2.fail.c2: Both Class 1 and Class 2 must add up to 12 students over the three fruits.
y-m-06-06.s.s2.ok.c3: In Class 1, apple is the winner.
y-m-06-06.s.s2.fail.c3: In Class 1, apple must be more than both tangerine and pear.
y-m-06-06.s.s2.ok.c4: In Class 2, tangerine is the winner.
y-m-06-06.s.s2.fail.c4: In Class 2, tangerine must be more than both apple and pear.
y-m-06-06.s.s2.ok.c5: When the two classes are combined, pear is more than both apple and tangerine. Jihu's statement is broken.
y-m-06-06.s.s2.fail.c5: When the two classes are combined, the number of pear must be greater than both the number of apple and the number of tangerine. Add up each fruit across the classes and compare.
y-m-06-06.s.s2.explain: For example, if Class 1 is apple 6, tangerine 1, pear 5 and Class 2 is apple 1, tangerine 6, pear 5, combined it is apple 7, tangerine 7, pear 10. Pear is not the winner in either class, but combined it is the most. So Jihu's statement is not always right.
y-m-06-06.s.s3.prompt: Write why pear, which was not the winner in either class, could become the winner when combined.
y-m-06-06.s.s3.hint.0: In the two tables you made, write the numbers of pear, apple, and tangerine side by side for each class.
y-m-06-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write the combined numbers, and find how many students the fruit that was the winner in one class had in the other class.
y-m-06-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you explain the reason using the numbers in your tables?
y-m-06-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that "when combined" and "in one class" are different?
y-m-06-06.s.s3.model.0: Pear was not the winner in either class, but 5 students in each class chose it evenly, so combined it is 10 and became more than apple or tangerine.
y-m-06-06.s.s3.model.1: Apple and tangerine are high in only one class and low in the other. Pear is fairly high in both classes, so it is the most when combined.

y-m-06-07.title: If the way of grouping changes, does the winner change too?
y-m-06-07.topic: Sorting: how the most changes depending on how things are grouped
y-m-06-07.goal: Realize that even with the same data, the thing that is most can change depending on what you group together and count as one, and let others know by stating how you grouped.
y-m-06-07.material:
The 26 students in our class each chose one game they most want to play during break time. 7 chose tag, 6 chose jump rope, 5 chose soccer, 4 chose basketball, and 4 chose dodgeball.
Jihu: "Tag has the most with 7, so the most popular game is tag."
Seoa: "If we group soccer, basketball, and dodgeball as ball games, that's 5+4+4=13, so ball games are the most popular."
The PE teacher wonders what game would be good to prepare after seeing this result.
y-m-06-07.thinking.0: Noticing that the result changes depending on the grouping rule
y-m-06-07.thinking.1: Making several groupings that fit the conditions
y-m-06-07.thinking.2: Telling the listener how you grouped
y-m-06-07.prereq.0: Reading and comparing numbers from a table
y-m-06-07.prereq.1: Reading the size of several numbers put together
y-m-06-07.s.s1.prompt: How can we view what Jihu and Seoa said? Choose the most fitting one.
y-m-06-07.s.s1.hint.0: Point out in the table which cells' numbers each of the two used.
y-m-06-07.s.s1.hint.1: Write side by side the biggest number when the same data is counted "one game at a time" and when it is counted "grouped by type."
y-m-06-07.s.s1.o.a: Only Seoa is right. If we decide to count games grouped by type, that is how it is.
y-m-06-07.s.s1.r.a: This saw counting each game separately as wrong from the start. What counts as one thing is up to how you decide, and if you state the way you decided, this thinking can be explained too.
y-m-06-07.s.s1.o.b: One of the two calculated a number wrong.
y-m-06-07.s.s1.r.b: 5+4+4 is 13 and 7 is a number in the table. Both people's numbers can be checked in the table.
y-m-06-07.s.s1.o.c: Both can be checked in the table, and the winner changes depending on the way of grouping and counting.
y-m-06-07.s.s1.r.c: This noticed that when the way of counting changes with the same data, the statement changes too.
y-m-06-07.s.s1.o.d: There is not enough data to say either one.
y-m-06-07.s.s1.r.d: From the table alone, both people's numbers can be checked. What is lacking is deciding "what is counted as one thing."
y-m-06-07.s.s1.o.e: Only Jihu is right. If we decide to count each game separately, that is how it is.
y-m-06-07.s.s1.r.e: This saw the way of grouping and counting as wrong from the start. If you state the way you decided, this thinking can be explained too.
y-m-06-07.s.s1.explain: Jihu's 7 and Seoa's 13 can both be checked with the numbers in the table. Counting each game separately, tag is the most, and counting grouped as ball games, ball games are the most. Either way, if you say "how you counted," both different statements are explained.
y-m-06-07.s.s1.acc.0: If we decide to count games grouped by type, Seoa's statement is right. But we have to state that we decided that way.
y-m-06-07.s.s1.acc.1: If we decide to count each game separately, Jihu's statement is right. But we have to state that we decided that way.
y-m-06-07.s.s2.prompt: The gym can hold at most 10 students in one place. The teacher wants to group exactly two of soccer, basketball, dodgeball, and jump rope into one team, so that the number of students in that team is more than tag (7 students) and at most 10. Write 1 if you choose it and 0 if you don't, and make two different groupings. (Number of students: soccer 5, basketball 4, dodgeball 4, jump rope 6)
y-m-06-07.s.s2.hint.0: Choose two, write the number of students, and check whether it is greater than 7 and not greater than 10.
y-m-06-07.s.s2.hint.1: Test what happens if you group the game with the most students together with the game with the fewest.
y-m-06-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Write only 1 if chosen and 0 if not chosen.
y-m-06-07.s.s2.ok.c3: The number of students is more than 7 and at most 10.
y-m-06-07.s.s2.fail.c3: Add up the numbers of students of the games you chose and check whether it is more than 7 and at most 10.
y-m-06-07.s.s2.explain: The groupings that fit the conditions are soccer+basketball (9 students), soccer+dodgeball (9 students), basketball+dodgeball (8 students), basketball+jump rope (10 students), and dodgeball+jump rope (10 students), five in all. Soccer+jump rope is 11 students, so it does not work. The number of students in the team changes depending on which two you group together.
y-m-06-07.s.s3.prompt: You want to tell the PE teacher what game would be good to prepare. State how you grouped and counted to get the result, and write it in two or three sentences.
y-m-06-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write the first sentence first, so that the teacher can tell "what was counted as one thing" by reading just one line of your writing.
y-m-06-07.s.s3.hint.1: Write down the biggest number that came from each of the two ways of counting.
y-m-06-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Teacher, if we count games ..., ...
y-m-06-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Can the teacher tell how the result was counted just by reading my writing?
y-m-06-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you present the results of both ways of counting, or, if you presented only one, did you say so?
y-m-06-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Do the numbers match the table?
y-m-06-07.s.s3.model.0: Teacher, if we count each game separately, tag has the most with 7 students. But if we group soccer, basketball, and dodgeball as ball games and count, it is 13 students, so ball games are the most. Please keep this in mind when you prepare balls.
y-m-06-07.s.s3.model.1: If we group and count ball games, soccer 5, basketball 4, and dodgeball 4 add up to 13 students, which is the most. But if we count each game name separately, tag with 7 students is the winner. It depends on how we count.
